headline.sentence: The belt moved freight 62% of the time. The other 11 minutes of 29 were lost to stops and gaps.

cards.title: The belt was stopped for a quarter of the session
cards.what: 12 stops of 10 seconds or more, 6.9 minutes in total. 4.5 of those minutes had freight sitting on the belt.
cards.why: While the belt was stopped, 35% of the people in view were waiting, against 19% while it flowed. A stop holds up everyone downstream of it.
cards.action: Find out what triggers each stop. The clips show awkward items (wire cages, long rolls) being handled on the belt during several of them; routing those off-belt is the first thing to test.
cards.next: Join this timeline to scan or warehouse-system data by time. Each stop then shows the freight scanned just before it, so the system can name the items that stop the belt without anyone having to ask. Not built here: this prototype has no scan data.

cards.title: The sorting team outran the supply from the truck
cards.what: 8 gaps of 10 seconds or more, 4.0 minutes in total, most of them in the first six minutes (belt flowing only 39% of that time).
cards.why: Headcount was highest during the gaps (5.4 people against 4.6 when flowing). Workers along the belt mainly take freight off it to sort, so an empty belt means the truck end is not feeding fast enough for the people waiting to sort.
cards.action: Look at the truck end first: one more person unloading, or fewer sorters during slow feed, would close the gap. A camera inside the dock door would confirm it.
cards.next: A camera at the dock door, or the truck arrival feed, turns supply from an inference into a measurement. The system could then flag a slow feed while it is happening, not afterwards.

cards.title: On average the line ran at less than half its own best minute
cards.what: Freight flow averaged 46% of the best sustained minute (from 22:16). Even while flowing, 41% of the belt surface was bare.
cards.why: The same people and the same belt have already shown the higher rate. The gap is steadiness, not speed.
cards.action: Use the best minute as the target rate and track minutes at or near it per session.
cards.next: Run on the live feed and show each bay its current rate against its own best minute, so a supervisor sees a drop as it starts.

cards.title: Unloading follows the belt: when it stops, people wait
cards.what: 65% of person-time was spent unloading (picking from the belt, carrying, returning), 13% on other activity and 22% waiting. While the belt flowed, 3.4 of 4.6 people were unloading.
cards.why: Unloading falls from 74% when the belt flows to 27% when it is stopped and empty, and waiting rises from 19% to 38%. People follow the belt, which points at the process, not the people. For 6% of the session three or more people were present with at most one unloading.
cards.action: Fix stops and gaps first. Then look at the other activity: some is stacking and staging, some is not work, and this camera cannot yet tell them apart.
cards.next: A model that looks at short clips, not only body position, to separate loading, stacking and idle movement. The review corrections already collected would score it.

cards.title: People could have been released to another bay, in short windows
cards.what: 3 windows where the belt was idle and about two people were waiting, lasting 27-42 seconds (3.8 person-minutes). 1 window where this bay was saturated with nobody waiting.
cards.why: The first six minutes had 5.6 people and the belt flowing 39% of the time; the rest had 4.3 people and 68%. Fewer people moved more freight, so the bigger win is the staffing level per phase, not second-by-second moves.
cards.action: Start by releasing one person during slow feed from the truck, and check that flow holds.
cards.next: With every bay measured the same way, the system matches one bay's release windows against another bay's pressure and alerts a supervisor when a move is worth the walk. The Site view page shows this with example data.

review.method: 20 five-second moments, 5 per belt state, picked at random (seed 7). Reviewer watched data/review_reel.mp4 with the system's labels drawn on and marked anything wrong.

belt_state.note: Moments 2 and 19 were labelled 'running empty' with one or two parcels on the belt. State renamed to 'running near-empty' (under 20% of the surface covered).

errors.note: one person at the far end shown working, was not
person at far left shown working, was not
three people shown working, none were (one seated)
person at the far end shown working, was not

worker_activity.direction: All six errors are waiting people counted as working. Reported waiting time is therefore a floor.
worker_activity.tuning_tried: Raising the motion threshold fixed 4 of the 6 but flipped 4 labels the reviewer had accepted; hand reach and torso lean did not separate the cases either. Threshold left at 0.12.
worker_activity.caveats: A reviewer flags what stands out, so 94% is an upper bound. 20 moments is a small sample.

rule_change_after_review.change: Reviewer's suggestion adopted: 'working' now means working the belt (a hand at the belt next to freight, plus 4 seconds either side for the pick, drop and return). Movement with no belt touch is 'active away from the belt'. Still is 'waiting'.
rule_change_after_review.effect_on_the_six_errors: None of the six is counted as working the belt any more: five fall in 'active away from the belt', one in 'waiting'.
rule_change_after_review.status: The new labels have not yet been reviewed by a person. data/review_reel.mp4 was regenerated with them for a second pass.
rule_change_after_review.second_correction: Reviewer spotted a pile-side worker clearing the belt shown as off belt. Cause: from this camera angle, hands held above the far side of the belt appear 30-50 px above the belt zone. Added a 'belt_reach' zone in config/zones.json that extends the hand-contact area on that side. Across 15 settings of the freight-proximity thresholds, belt-work share stayed between 57% and 65%.
rule_change_after_review.third_correction: Reviewer spotted a far-end worker carrying a box shown as not unloading. Added: (1) the unloading state continues after a belt touch for as long as the person keeps moving, up to 10 s, to cover the carry; (2) the hand-contact zone extends 30 px past the far end of the belt. Sensitivity: across the geometry and threshold settings tried, the unloading share ranged from 62% to 77%, so treat it as approximate. Display names changed to Unloading / Other activity / Waiting.
rule_change_after_review.fourth_correction: Round 4 corrections added to data/review_labels.json (13 person-level corrections in total) with a scoring script, analytics/evaluate.py. Added: a 'leaning' detail (still hand on the belt counts as waiting), a fetch-to-belt rule (covers loading from a cage), a stricter false-person filter, and analytics/safety.py for belt crossings and leaning events. Score: 12 of 13 corrections satisfied. The miss is a man standing at the dock door gesturing beside a loaded belt: pose data cannot tell that from handling. Loading and unloading are not yet distinguished, and smoking cannot be detected from pose.
